segments.text: Start at the input. Both cores receive the same 64-bit AXI stream. That stream can come
from the processing system, Ethernet ingress, or the block RAM replay reader.
In the quartz integration, a local adapter feeds one byte per clock into two full block buffers.
One fills while the other feeds the hash state. 24 permutation rounds produce the result,
which is copied into a separate digest register. The compact core uses that same
stream interface. It captures up to 8 bytes at a time, then absorbs them directly into
the hash state with an aligned exclusive OR. The two full block buffers disappear. The
digest comes directly from the held state, so that separate register disappears too.
Capture and absorption still take separate cycles. The 24-round permutation is unchanged.
Two smaller changes simplify the compact core further.
First, padding. Compare this project's earlier wide core with the compact version.
Previously, a variable index selected from all 25 state lanes. The compact version decodes the destination locally across only the 17 rate lanes that padding can touch.
The eight capacity lanes remain in the hash state. Padding leaves them alone.
Second, input validation. The earlier design checked the byte mask and end-of-message flag
on the state update control path. The compact core records that check while capturing the input.
On the next cycle, a bad word is rejected before absorption. These changes reduce surrounding
logic. They preserve the hash algorithm and the simulated cycle count.
The speedup is quartz's time divided by the compact core's time. One means equal speed.
For large messages, the compact core reaches about 2.4 times the throughput.
That advantage stays as the message keeps growing.
